newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania asks for "intensive" election monitoring.
newsitem.headline: Albania asks for "intensive" election monitoring.

text.p: Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, seeking to end a long-running crisis over elections, asked the international community on Wednesday for "intensive" monitoring of the vote.
Fino has sought to persuade political parties to lift a threatened boycott of the June 29 elections, sorely needed to stop Albania slipping back into anarchy.
After day-long talks with the parties and a government meeting, Fino sent a letter to European Union envoy Franz Vranitzky asking for international monitors to oversee the whole electoral process.

"The final solution to ensure free, fair and equal elections where all would participate and not contest the result would be to guarantee intensive monitoring of all levels of the electoral process in Albania by the international community," he said in the letter, read on television.
The elections are intended to restore order after Albania was engulfed earlier this year by riots and looting sparked by the collapse of dubious investment schemes that bankrupted many people.
Fino's letter did not explain what he meant by intensive monitoring but politicians said he wanted the same kind of supervision as in troubled and divided areas such as Bosnia.

One politician said this would mean measures such as the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) taking charge of compiling voter lists and voter registration and stationing a monitor in every polling station.
Most parties said they would refuse to contest the elections after accusing President Sali Berisha and his former ruling Democratic Party of passing election laws favouring a Democratic victory.
Fatos Nano, leader of the Socialists, the second largest party, said full monitoring would be enough to persuade his party to stand in the elections, even under the current laws.
"We have to wait and I hope for a quick answer (from Vranitzky)," he said.
Although Albania is far calmer now, sporadic violence still erupts and people are killed on an almost daily basis.
Italian Prime Minister Romani Prodi, whose country leads a multinational force protecting humanitarian aid, voiced support for Fino and said he expected a break in the political deadlock soon.
"The differences among the parties are very small now," Prodi told a news conference in Budapest. "I am confident that we can have some positive steps in the next days or so."
